chunks.text: ILKIN ISLER, Ph.D. ilkinisler@gmail.com LinkedIn Google Scholar GitHub ilkinisler.com

Senior AI Engineer working in a forward-deployed role: meets with business teams, scopes complex business needs, and builds the AI solution from first prototype to trusted production. Builds models, not just uses them: Ph.D. in Computer Science focused on designing novel neural network architectures, with hands-on work across computer vision, NLP, LLMs, agentic systems, automation, and dataset creation.

Built RAG, hallucination detection, and evaluation systems and an enterprise AI platform from scratch, and co-developed an enterprise data ingestion pipeline for structured and unstructured documents, all designed to enterprise security and governance standards. Leads an AI engineering team across AI infrastructure, finance automation, and cost estimating.
Languages & Cloud: Python, SQL (database schema design, data modeling), Azure, Google Cloud (Cloud Run)
LLMs & Frameworks: Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, LlamaIndex, LangChain, LangGraph, FastAPI
Search & Vector Databases: Neo4j (graph database), Azure Cosmos DB, SQLite FTS5 (full-text search), pgvector (Postgres), Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Chroma, FAISS

LLM & Agentic AI: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Hybrid Search (BM25 + Vector), Data and Document Ingestion Pipelines (structured and unstructured data), Temporal Knowledge Graphs, Entity and Relationship Extraction, Graph-Traversal Retrieval, Multi-Agent Systems, Agent Orchestration, Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server Development, Function Calling and Tool Use, Agent Skills, LLM Integration, Prompt Engineering, Vision-Language Model Fine-Tuning

Evaluation & Trustworthy AI: Hallucination Detection, Groundedness Evaluation, Vectara HHEM, Citation Verification, LLM-as-Judge, RAGAS, DeepEval, BERTScore, ROUGE, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), Benchmark Dataset Creation, Synthetic Data Generation for RAG Evals, Failure Analysis, Uncertainty Quantification, Explainable AI, AI Safety and Governance

Deep Learning & Computer Vision: PyTorch, Multi-GPU Distributed Training (PyTorch DDP), Multi-Source Dataset Curation, Data Augmentation, MONAI, Neural Network Architecture Design, Self-Supervised Pretraining, Transfer Learning & Fine-Tuning (Swin UNETR, foundation models), Custom Loss Function Design, Medical Image Segmentation, Segmentation Metrics (Dice, HD95), NLP, Anomaly Detection

AI Platform & Architecture: Enterprise AI Architecture, Human-in-the-Loop Systems, Access Control (RBAC, ABAC), Model-Serving APIs, Workflow Automation, CI/CD Pipelines, Observability and Monitoring (Azure Application Insights, logging dashboards), AI-Assisted Development (Codex)

Designed from scratch, as solution architect, human-in-the-loop AI tools for finance reporting and forecasting that replaced a frequently reworked, file-per-project spreadsheet process, then led the developers who implemented them into production; the tools unify project finance data in one source of truth, surface the top cost drivers each month, and flag transaction risk, with the analyst in control of every number.

Architected from scratch a human-in-the-loop cost-estimating system of purpose-built AI tools and lead its delivery as solution architect: the tools generate scope from design drawings, structure messy, non-standardized scope lists into estimates and track how they change, and retrieve everything previously paid for an item; won over skeptical estimators by replicating their Excel workflows first and adding automation as trust grew.

chunks.text: The Mind to Move Mountains

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: Ilkin Isler '22MS '25PhD left the familiarity of home in Turkey to study AI at UCF - a daring choice that resulted in research improving the assessment of cancerous tumors and supporting better patient care.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: Nothing motivates Ilkin Isler '22MS '25PhD quite like this phrase: “It can't be done.”

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: When Isler says candidly, “Working on my Ph.D. is the most difficult thing I've ever faced,” there's a montage of difficult things in her life to consider - physical and mental, past and present.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: For example, in August 2025, the recent computer science doctoral graduate began work as a senior artificial intelligence (AI) engineer at Universal Creative. Her role involved analyzing complex white papers and developing state-of-the-art AI systems from scratch - all for the purpose of improving the safety of park guests.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: “I find solutions for high-risk applications,” Isler says, “which is a good description for what I love to do.”

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: “… when I hear something can't be done, it motivates me to make it happen.” - Ilkin Isler '22MS '25PhD

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: The fact that her work requires fortitude also fits Isler well. In high school in Turkey, she once walked into a gym “just for something to do.” A trainer immediately suggested she head to the cardio area, where she'd blend in easily. Isler, however, saw the powerlifting space and thought, “ That's what I want to do.”

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: “I had to teach myself how to do [powerlifting],” she says. “People probably thought I'd give up, but when I hear something can't be done, it motivates me to make it happen.”

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: Self-taught and competing despite her small frame, Isler went on to become a European powerlifting champion.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: All of this is important for understanding the person who, while studying at UCF, helped develop an AI model to assess cancerous tumors.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Using Computer Imaging to Enhance Patient Care
chunks.text: Guided by a team of advisors, Isler came up with a way to feed medical imaging into an algorithm that measures shapes and textures with more speed, precision and consistency than is currently possible. Given such accurate information, an oncologist could make quicker, more confident decisions - improving overall patient care.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Using Computer Imaging to Enhance Patient Care
chunks.text: “… [Ilkin's] work helps push the field forward in an important and timely way.” - David Mohaisen, UCF computer science professor

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Using Computer Imaging to Enhance Patient Care
chunks.text: “The problem she chose to work on is inherently difficult for several reasons,” says David Mohaisen, UCF computer science professor and one of her advisors. “Medical imaging is a high-stakes domain where errors have serious clinical consequences.”

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Using Computer Imaging to Enhance Patient Care
chunks.text: “It's also a mature and crowded research area, with competitive works focusing on incremental benchmark gains rather than addressing deeper issues, such as reliability, uncertainty and clinical integration,” Mohaisen continues. “Instead of chasing marginal improvements, Ilkin focused on meaningful outcomes. Her work helps push the field forward in an important and timely way.”

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Using Computer Imaging to Enhance Patient Care
chunks.text: Yet the breakthrough alone, and the work that went into it, does not fully capture what Isler faced at the dizzying start of her doctorate journey.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Taking a Chance to Change Her Life and Others
chunks.text: Isler arrived from Turkey with two suitcases and a hotel reservation near UCF.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Taking a Chance to Change Her Life and Others
chunks.text: “My mom filled one of the suitcases with Turkish food,” Isler says. She can laugh now, but at the time, she had no clear path beyond the airport. “I had to figure everything out.”

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Taking a Chance to Change Her Life and Others
chunks.text: A few years earlier, she traveled across the globe to UCF as an undergraduate, having earned a competitive internship in the Synthetic Reality Lab, where she worked with Pegasus Professor Charles Hughes and then computer engineering doctoral student Kamran Ali '21PhD on facial expression recognition.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Taking a Chance to Change Her Life and Others
chunks.text: “She committed herself to the research,” Hughes says, “and even contributed to writing and editing the resulting report after she returned to Turkey.”

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Taking a Chance to Change Her Life and Others
chunks.text: Days away from starting doctorate-level research, with all her belongings in a single piece of luggage, Isler would do what she does best: find a way. She moved from the hotel to an unfurnished apartment.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Taking a Chance to Change Her Life and Others
chunks.text: But with her, Isler brought two specific interests to her postgraduate research at UCF. Her mother, a dentist in Turkey, inspired an interest in medical advancement. Her father, a computer science professor, recognized in his daughter the curiosity and determination required for the field.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Taking a Chance to Change Her Life and Others
chunks.text: “If I know an idea can be impactful, I'll do whatever is necessary to make it a reality,” she says. “The higher the stakes, the more driven I become.”

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Taking a Chance to Change Her Life and Others
chunks.text: Those stakes led her to focus on medical imaging solutions for cancer care worldwide. Without a medical background, she collaborated with doctors. It helped that she never looked at her research as an academic exercise. She wanted only to deliver something trustworthy that clinicians everywhere could use to eliminate gray areas in image analysis.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.section: Taking a Chance to Change Her Life and Others
chunks.text: “I've been fortunate to work with many doctoral students over the years, and Ilkin stands out on multiple levels,” says Mohaisen, pointing out her motivation, energy and curiosity, before adding: “I'd say she is among the most driven.”

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: By now, the source of Isler's uncommon drive is clear. Every time someone showed skepticism about her powerlifting, she responded by breaking a national record. Although she could have attended a private college in Turkey, where she would have been surrounded by familiar language and culture, she instead chose to move across the world to study AI.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: There's one more motivation that consistently guides her: others.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: Isler considers her greatest accomplishment in powerlifting to be the doors she helped open for others in Turkey to try any form of fitness they choose. And she says she would gladly move to another continent again, with just a suitcase and her AI skills, if it meant helping improve the lives of others.

chunks.source_title: The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News)
chunks.text: “When I look back, I can see that I've often traded comfort for growth,” she says, “and I will not hesitate to do it again.”
I moved from Turkey to the United States to pursue AI at UCF, where I earned my MS in Computer Science in 2022 and my PhD in 2025.

At work I build enterprise AI systems: an in-house AI platform for deploying, orchestrating, and governing AI tools, agents, and multi-agent workflows (including MCP servers, tool calling, and agent skills), LLM evaluation and hallucination detection pipelines, and human-in-the-loop tools for finance and cost estimating. On my own time I build personal AI assistants for home workflows and daily automation, and this site's grounded assistant.

One of my two main initiatives at work is AI for finance reporting and forecasting. Finance teams kept a separate, frequently reworked spreadsheet for every project, so monthly reporting meant hours of manual consolidation. I built, from scratch, human-in-the-loop AI tools that bring project finance data into one adaptable source of truth, surface the top cost drivers each month, flag transactions worth a closer look, and support forecasting while the analyst stays in control of every number. I started from how analysts actually close a month, kept every output reviewable, and evaluated new methods before they reached the team.

My other main initiative is AI-assisted cost estimating, which I lead along with its developers. Estimating large, one-of-a-kind projects depends on deep expertise and messy, non-standardized inputs, and the estimators were skeptical at first. We built from scratch a suite of purpose-built, human-in-the-loop tools that read design drawings to draft scope, turn messy scope lists into structured estimates and track how they change, and retrieve everything previously paid for an item. Instead of replacing their Excel workflows, the tools accept their existing files and return results in the same format; we started with small validated wins and added automation as trust grew. The conversation moved from whether it would work to what else we could automate. I am also building, from scratch, a project-intelligence tool on a temporal knowledge-graph architecture similar to Graphiti: project decks, schedules, and budget updates are ingested as episodes, an LLM extracts entities and relationships into a graph, facts keep their history instead of being overwritten, and retrieval combines semantic search, keyword search, and graph traversal. It gives senior leadership one view of what changed across a project and how it affects budgets, plans, and schedules.

My research is about building AI that people can rely on, which starts with knowing when a model is wrong. During my PhD I designed 3D neural network architectures, loss functions, and uncertainty quantification methods for tumor and organ-at-risk segmentation; my self-supervised and uncertainty-guided approaches achieved state-of-the-art results at publication. Today I apply the same idea to LLMs: retrieval-augmented generation, hallucination detection, groundedness and citation checks, and evaluation pipelines that decide when an answer can be trusted, or when the system should decline to answer.

Selected publications with links: Pancreas CT/MRI segmentation (2025) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2024.103382; Power-VR (2022) https://doi.org/10.1002/cav.2045; Uncertainty-Guided Tumor Segmentation (2025) https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2504.12215; OAR and Tumor Segmentation with UQ (2023) https://doi.org/10.1109/ICECCME57830.2023.10252269; Enhancing OAR Segmentation (2022) https://doi.org/10.1117/12.2611498; Facial Expression Translation (2019) https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1910.05595; Generative AI in Medical Imaging (2024) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72787-0_17. Full list: https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ZgPdlJ0AAAAJ&hl=en.

My powerlifting PRs are Squat 355 lbs, Bench 200 lbs, and Deadlift 475 lbs. I am a European powerlifting champion (1st Place Overall at the IPSU European Championship) and a two-time Overall Champion of Türkiye. I am still holding deadlift records in Turkiye since 2020 and in Florida since 2022. These include both junior and open records, and I broke both while I was a junior. Sources: USAPL records database https://usapl.liftingdatabase.com/records-default?priority=0&recordtypeid=120382&categoryid=&weightclassid= and IPF Turkiye records https://powerlifting.org.tr/turkiye-rekorlari.
My featured story is The Mind to Move Mountains (UCF News): https://www.ucf.edu/news/the-mind-to-move-mountains/.

You can reach me at ilkinisler@gmail.com. LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/ilkinsevgiisler/. Google Scholar: https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ZgPdlJ0AAAAJ&hl=en. GitHub: https://github.com/ilkinisler.

This assistant answers only from my resume, the UCF News feature, and these first-party facts. It uses hybrid retrieval (BM25-style keyword matching plus embedding similarity), declines to answer when retrieval confidence is low instead of guessing, and checks that each answer sentence is supported by a source. I built it as a small, public example of the grounded, hallucination-aware systems I build at work.
